title: Zerodha's New Life Cycle Funds: A Practical Guide
description: Zerodha Fund House has launched India's first life cycle mutual funds, a new category introduced by SEBI in February 2026. These target-date funds automatical.

faq.q: What is a life cycle fund?
faq.a: A life cycle fund, also known as a target-date fund, is a type of mutual fund that automatically adjusts its asset allocation over time. It typically starts with higher equity exposure when the target date is far away and gradually shifts towards more conservative debt instruments as the target date approaches.

faq.q: How do these funds adjust risk?
faq.a: These funds follow a "glide path," a predefined strategy that systematically reduces exposure to volatile assets like equities and increases allocation to stable assets like debt as the investor gets closer to their specified target date, thus de-risking the portfolio.

faq.q: Are life cycle funds suitable for everyone?
faq.a: Life cycle funds are best suited for investors with a clear, long-term financial goal (like retirement) who prefer a hands-off approach to asset allocation and rebalancing. They may not be ideal for those who wish to actively manage their portfolio or have very specific, non-standard financial needs.

faq.q: What are the tax implications of investing in life cycle funds?
faq.a: The taxation of life cycle funds will generally follow the rules applicable to equity-oriented or debt-oriented mutual funds, depending on their asset allocation at the time of redemption. For equity-oriented funds (over 65% equity), long-term capital gains (LTCG) above ₹1 lakh are taxed at 10% without indexation, and short-term capital gains (STCG) at 15%. For debt-oriented funds, capital gains are taxed as per income tax slab rates after indexation benefit for long-term holdings.

faq.q: Can I switch between different life cycle funds?
faq.a: While technically possible, switching between different target-date life cycle funds (e.g., from a 2040 fund to a 2050 fund) would involve redemption from one and investment into another, incurring capital gains tax and potentially exit loads. It's generally advisable to choose the fund that aligns with your longest-term goal initially.

faq.q: How do these differ from regular balanced funds?
faq.a: Regular balanced funds (or aggressive hybrid funds) maintain a relatively fixed equity-debt allocation (e.g., 60-40 or 75-25) throughout their life. Life cycle funds, on the other hand, dynamically change this allocation over time, gradually becoming more conservative as they approach a specific target date, which is their core distinguishing feature.
